title: The mini-rhythm: example, code, check
idea: Review lap. Name the tiny loop you already use: work an example, write the print code, check the output matches. No new tool.

exercises.prompt: You've learned a tiny rhythm for small 'show this' tasks. What are the three steps, in order?
options: Example by hand -> write the code -> check the output
exercises.explanation: First work an example by hand, then write the print code, then check the real output against your example. You already know each piece.

exercises.prompt: This unit teaches a brand-new tool you haven't seen before.
exercises.explanation: No new tool here. This is a review lap — we just loop back over print, examples, and checking.

exercises.prompt: The task is: show the word Hello. First step of the rhythm — the example. What should the output be?
exercises.explanation: The expected output is just: Hello. Working the example first tells you what the code must produce.

exercises.prompt: Second step — the code. Build an instruction to show: Hello
exercises.explanation: print("Hello") — the word in quotes, inside the brackets. Same print you met in Unit 1.

exercises.prompt: Third step — check. You run print("Hello") and it shows Hello. Your example said Hello. So...
options: It passes — the output matches the example
exercises.explanation: Output matches the hand example, so it passes. That is exactly what checking means.

exercises.prompt: Put the mini-rhythm steps in the right order.
exercises.explanation: Example first (so you know the target), then code, then check against the example.

exercises.prompt: The hand example is what you compare the real output against when you check.
exercises.explanation: The example is your target. Checking is just: does the output match the example?

exercises.prompt: Which instruction correctly shows the word Welcome?
exercises.explanation: Lowercase print, matching quotes, both brackets. A quick review from Unit 1.

exercises.prompt: Why do we work the example BEFORE writing the code?
options: So we know the right answer to check against
exercises.explanation: If you don't know the expected output first, you have nothing to check against. Example first, always.

exercises.prompt: You finished naming the rhythm. What can you do now?
options: Take a tiny 'show this' task and run example -> code -> check
exercises.explanation: You can run the full mini-circle on a small task. The rest of this unit is practice loops.
